steps.label: Zeeman effect
lines: Zeeman effect: the splitting of spectral
lines into several lines when the source is
steps.why: The magnetic quantum number m fixes how an orbital is oriented in space. A magnetic field gives these orientations slightly different energies, so one line becomes several.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two fields. Zeeman is the magnetic one.
Writing that the lines shift instead of split. The single line becomes several lines.
steps.memory_tip: Zeeman and magnet both carry the letter m.
steps.margin_note: Name the field and say split. Those two words carry the mark.

steps.label: Stark effect

lines.text: Stark effect: splitting of spectral lines in an electric field

lines: Both effects show that an external field
splits one spectral line into several lines.
steps.why: The two effects are asked together because both show line splitting in an external field, but they do not share one explanation. The Zeeman effect comes from the magnetic quantum number m, which fixes how an orbital is oriented in space, so a magnetic field gives those orientations different energies. The Stark effect comes from the interaction of the electric field with the electric dipole moment of the atom. An earlier version of this card ended with the line 'Both effects are explained by the magnetic quantum number m'; that line was corrected on 2026-08-25, because m explains the Zeeman effect only. Bohr's model cannot explain either effect, and that is one of its listed limitations.
common_mistakes: Writing that the Stark effect happens in a magnetic field.
Saying the magnetic quantum number m explains both effects. It explains the Zeeman effect only; the Stark effect comes from the electric dipole moment of the atom.
steps.memory_tip: Two fields, two names: magnetic is Zeeman, electric is Stark.
steps.margin_note: The last line states what the two effects have in common: an external field splits one line into several.

insider_note: The pair is always asked together. Write one line each and name the field correctly, because swapping the two fields loses both marks.
